title: Rotting Oranges
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning the entire grid every minute versus a multi-source BFS processed round by round.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a grid of 0 (empty), 1 (fresh orange), and 2 (rotten orange), every minute any fresh orange 4-directionally adjacent to a rotten orange becomes rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes until no fresh orange remains, or -1 if that is impossible.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Something spreads simultaneously from MULTIPLE sources, minute by minute\"","A multi-source BFS: seed the queue with every source at once, and the BFS depth (level) directly corresponds to elapsed time"]]}

blocks.text: Since ALL rotten oranges spread simultaneously each minute, this is a MULTI-SOURCE BFS: seed the initial queue with every rotten orange's position at once (all at "minute 0"), then process the queue level by level, exactly as a normal BFS would, with each level corresponding to one elapsed minute. This naturally and correctly models the simultaneous spread without needing separate tracking per source.

blocks.title: Analogy: An Infection Spreading Simultaneously From Multiple Initial Carriers
blocks.text: Picture an infection that spreads to any adjacent healthy person once per time step, starting from several initially infected people scattered around a room simultaneously. Tracking the spread level by level (everyone infected in the SAME time step processed together) correctly models how many steps it takes for the infection to reach everyone reachable.

blocks.caption: Multi-source BFS from all rotten oranges simultaneously; BFS depth equals elapsed minutes

blocks.text: Result: -1 (the orange at bottom-left is isolated by empty cells, never reachable).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Scan the grid once, collecting the positions of every initially rotten orange into a BFS queue simultaneously, and counting the total number of fresh oranges.

Observation 2: Process the queue in ROUNDS (levels): each round represents exactly one minute, during which every currently-queued rotten orange spreads to its 4-directional fresh neighbors, turning them rotten and decrementing the fresh count.

Observation 3: Continue processing rounds as long as the queue is non-empty AND fresh oranges remain; each completed round increments the elapsed minutes counter.

Observation 4: After the BFS finishes, if the fresh count has reached 0, the elapsed minutes counter is the answer; otherwise, some fresh oranges were never reachable, so return -1.
This leads to a multi-source BFS, seeded with every initially rotten orange, processed round by round, counting elapsed minutes.
Simulate minute by minute, rescanning the ENTIRE grid at each minute to find and rot every fresh orange adjacent to a currently rotten one.
Why the code is written this way

items: Rescanning the grid each minute directly simulates the spreading process.
This costs a full grid rescan for EVERY minute elapsed, wasteful; a BFS processes each cell exactly once overall, regardless of how many minutes elapse.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((rows times cols) times minutes elapsed), since the grid is rescanned every minute.
Space: O(1) extra beyond the grid.
Limitation: a multi-source BFS processes each cell exactly once overall, regardless of how many minutes elapse, avoiding repeated full-grid rescans.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Scan the grid once, seeding a BFS queue with every initially rotten orange's position, and counting the total fresh oranges. While the queue is non-empty AND fresh oranges remain, process one ROUND: for every position currently in the queue, check its 4 neighbors; any fresh neighbor becomes rotten (decrementing fresh count) and is added to the NEXT round's queue. After processing a full round, increment the elapsed minutes counter. Once the loop ends, return the minutes counter if fresh reached 0, otherwise return -1.
Use a multi-source BFS, seeded with every initially rotten orange, processed round by round.

blocks.text: Seeding the BFS queue with ALL initially rotten oranges at once correctly models them all rotting neighbors SIMULTANEOUSLY, and processing the queue in discrete rounds (using the standard "snapshot queue size" BFS technique) correctly corresponds one-to-one with elapsed minutes; the loop naturally terminates either when every reachable fresh orange has been rotted (fresh reaches 0) or when the queue empties with fresh oranges still remaining (meaning they were never reachable, correctly signaling -1).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times cols), each cell processed once.
Space: O(rows times cols) for the queue in the worst case.

blocks.text: Rotting Oranges is the canonical multi-source BFS problem: seeding the queue with ALL sources simultaneously correctly models parallel spreading.

items: Seeding the BFS with only ONE rotten orange instead of all of them, incorrectly modeling sequential rather than simultaneous spreading.
Forgetting to check for remaining fresh oranges at the end, incorrectly returning the elapsed minutes even when some oranges were never actually reachable.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "seed the BFS with every source simultaneously, since they all spread in parallel" is the key insight that distinguishes multi-source BFS from a single-source BFS run multiple times.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "something spreads simultaneously from multiple starting points, minute by minute", think: multi-source BFS, seeding the queue with every source at once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The repeated-rescanning brute force costs O((rows times cols) times minutes); the multi-source BFS costs O(rows times cols), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: multi-source BFS, seeding the queue with every source simultaneously.
Core Idea: process the queue in rounds; each round corresponds to exactly one minute of simultaneous spreading.
Time: O((rows times cols) times minutes) for the brute force, O(rows times cols) for the BFS approach.
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(rows times cols) for the BFS approach.
Most Important Observation: seeding with ALL sources at once correctly models simultaneous, parallel spreading.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, foundational medium-level BFS problem.
One line memory trick: seed with every source, count the rounds.
